title: 1,300 Eyes on the Emerald City
dek: Seattle's police camera web is bigger than anyone told you, and until now nobody needed a reason to look.
body: Wave at the lamppost. It might wave back. According to the city's own Office of Inspector General, more than 1,300 cameras are now plugged into or registered with the Seattle Police Department's Real Time Crime Center. That's not a typo, and it's not a conspiracy theory scrawled on a bus shelter on Aurora. It's the annual review, released at the start of October.

Here's the breakdown. 427 of those cameras can feed live video to the cops: 308 belong to SPD, 96 to the transportation department and 23 are privately owned. Another 893 private cameras are registered with the department without a live feed, which means police know where they are and can ask for the footage.

The part that should make your neck itch: the Axon Fusus software running the whole show didn't require a case number or any reason at all before an analyst pulled up a camera. The Inspector General recommended fixing that, and SPD agreed. Better late than never, but think about how long never lasted.
> More than 1,300 cameras. No case number required to look.

To be fair to the people watching, analysts saved 1,659 clips as evidence in 2025, and the review found 98 percent were tied to high-priority calls or serious and violent crime. The 21 cameras bolted up around the Stadium District for the World Cup are still there, switched off. For now.

What the review can't tell you is whether any of it works. Nobody knows yet if the cameras actually cut crime. A separate study with the University of Pennsylvania is due at the end of 2027. Until then, we're all extras in a very long pilot episode. Smile.

sources.title: New report finds Seattle police camera network larger than previously reported

title: ICE Still Has Your Driver's License on Speed Dial
dek: Washington swore it shut the door. A UW report says immigration agents found the windows, the side gate and the doggy door.
body: Washington passed the Keep Washington Working Act back in 2019 to stop state agencies from handing your private details to federal immigration agents over civil matters. Nice law. Lovely sentiment. According to a new report from the University of Washington Center for Human Rights, it leaks like a Pioneer Square basement in November.

The report, 'Stopping the DMV-to-DHS Data Pipeline,' dropped October 13. It maps four ways driver data still reaches immigration agents: straight out of state databases, through the Nlets interstate police network, through local cops, and through private data brokers who will sell anything to anyone with a credit card.

The numbers are not small. The researchers counted 3,696,147 driver and vehicle data searches from January 2025 through May 2026. Gov. Bob Ferguson's office says it blocked 174,349 queries from immigration agents between November 2025 and October 2026. It didn't say how many got through.
> We need accountability, and we need leadership now, not months from now. (Guillermo Rivera, Eastside For All)

Some doors did get slammed. ICE's enforcement and investigations arms were cut off from Nlets earlier, and five Border Patrol usernames were blocked as of September 18. But UWCHR director Angelina Godoy compared the system to sharing a Netflix password with family. Block one login and the account is still wide open.
So here's the Sinner's advice, free of charge: your license is a document, not a diary. Know your rights, know who's asking, and ask Olympia why a 2019 promise still needs patching in 2026.

sources.title: ICE Still Outsmarting Washington's Driver Data Protections

title: Welcome to the 'Unfund' Budget
dek: A $175 million hole, a mayor with new priorities and four councilmembers who discovered the word 'unfund.'
body: Seattle is $175 million in the red, and City Hall has decided the best way to deal with it is a vocabulary contest. In a budget session this week, centrist councilmembers Bob Kettle, Maritza Rivera, Dan Strauss and Rob Saka accused Mayor Katie Wilson of writing an 'unfund' budget, one they say starves encampment removals, graffiti cleanup, park bathroom scrubbing and transportation projects.

Dig into the actual cuts and it gets funnier. The Unified Care Team, the crew that clears encampments, would lose two and a half administrative positions. Those positions have never been filled. Last year's budget language pegged the team at $30 million and 116 people. Cutting a job nobody holds is the municipal equivalent of breaking up with someone you never dated.
> we can't even get our own bathhouse in order! (Councilmember Rob Saka)

Meanwhile the mayor is proposing 10 new portable public restrooms, which in this town counts as radical infrastructure. And the transportation fund is reportedly running an average deficit of $41 million a month this year. That one is not a joke, even if the parking signs are.

Budget season always turns council chambers into a sitcom. This year's episode has a twist: the deficit is real, the bathrooms are portable, and everyone is fighting over things that may not exist. Stay tuned, and maybe bring your own toilet paper.

sources.title: Council Critics Accuse Wilson of Creating "the Unfund Budget"

title: Eight Million for the Weirdos
dek: Seattle's artists want a slice of the cops' raise. The math is simple. The politics never are.
body: Mayor Wilson's proposed budget hands the Seattle Police Department a $68 million increase. An open letter from the city's arts community, started by Julie Chang Shulman, asks for $8 million of that to go to the people who actually make this town worth living in.

The letter's pitch: art and cultural placemaking is public safety infrastructure. As of KIRO's October 5 report, more than 115 organizations and over 800 individuals had signed on. They point to this summer's World Cup, when the city handed out $3.6 million through 120 grants for 80 public art projects, and to June, which went down as Seattle's first month without a homicide in roughly five decades. To be clear, nobody has proven the murals did that. But nobody's proven they didn't, either.
> art and cultural placemaking is public safety infrastructure. (the open letter)

Where does the police money go? According to The Stranger, about $53.8 million covers the new police guild contract and about $12.6 million pays for 66 officers hired this year. Councilmember Bob Kettle says the increase doesn't go far enough.

Without the World Cup money, the city's arts spending would actually drop $2.1 million next year under the mayor's plan. So the question for City Hall is simple: was FIFA summer a fluke or a blueprint? Seattle's weirdos are waiting for an answer, and they've already painted the protest signs.

sources.title: Open letter calls on Seattle City Council to fund arts with portion of increased police funding
Why Can't Seattle Fund the Arts Like It's FIFA Every Year?

title: The Carrot and the Cage
dek: Community court is back with a new name. So is the hammer.
body: Remember community court? Former City Attorney Ann Davison killed it in 2023. Her successor, Erika Evans, just brought it back from the dead as 'Connection Court,' for low-level stuff like shoplifting and public drug use. Retiring Judge Willie Gregory runs it for the rest of the year.
The deal: stay out of trouble for 90 days and complete two kinds of services, like addiction counseling or job training, and you walk. That's the carrot.

Here's the cage. A new program called HiPRO, short for High-Priority Repeat Offenses, targets anyone with more than three misdemeanors in 90 days or more than six in six months. Those folks can't get diversion, and prosecutors will push for what the city calls 'aggravated jail sentences.'
> we hold accountable those who continue to cause harm. (Andre Sayles, interim police chief)

The public defenders see a hole in the plan you could drive a Metro bus through. Katie Hurley of King County's Department of Public Defense says about 30 percent of people miss municipal court dates because they don't have an address for the notices. Her verdict on the new court: there's no connection to housing.
So the city built a court called Connection that may not connect people to the one thing that keeps them out of court. Seattle irony, served daily.

sources.title: Revived Community Court Will be Paired With Punitive New "High-Priority" Program

title: Seattle Bans the Robot Price Tag
dek: Your groceries were getting a personalized markup. Now that's illegal here, starting in 2027.
body: You and the guy behind you at Safeway may not be paying the same price for the same eggs. Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative found Instacart prices swung by as much as 23 percent between customers at the same store. At one Seattle Safeway, the identical cart cost anywhere from $114.34 to $123.93, depending on who was buying.

The City Council has had enough. It passed a first-in-the-nation city ordinance banning 'algorithmic-based price discrimination' by grocery chains and delivery apps. It covers online prices, personalized in-store discounts and those creepy electronic shelf labels that can change in a blink.
> prevent AI-assisted price gouging (Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck)

The ban hits chains with at least 20 stores worldwide, plus delivery and online ordering services. Mayor Wilson planned to sign it in early October. Shoppers, she said, don't want their data fed into algorithms that decide how much they pay.
The catch: it doesn't kick in until September 1, 2027. So for the next year, shop like you're being watched, because you are. Clear your cookies, and maybe buy your kale with cash.

sources.title: Seattle to be 1st city to ban grocery prices set by algorithm

title: Pink Slip City
dek: Twenty rounds of tech layoffs and counting. The badge-and-lanyard boom is going flat.
body: Count them on your fingers and toes, then borrow a friend's. Axios tallied at least 20 publicly announced rounds of tech cuts hitting Seattle-area workers this year.

The big ones: about 2,200 Washington jobs at Amazon, 1,395 at Meta and 605 at Microsoft. Then the drip. Since early August: Oracle 359, Amazon another 121, Qualtrics 117, Uber 93, Zillow 91, T-Mobile 77, TikTok 75, Salesforce 59 and Google 52.

Of 9,027 workers named in layoff notices through August 18, 6,766 worked in the information sector, according to the local Workforce Development Council. King County's July unemployment rate hit 4.9 percent, above the state's 4.5.
> Flat is unusual for this traditionally high-growth sector (Anneliese Vance-Sherman, state labor economist)

Vance-Sherman says the sector is in the midst of a shift, which is economist for 'buckle up.' For the rest of us, it means the guy who priced you out of your Fremont one-bedroom might be on the couch next to you at the Blue Moon by spring. Be nice. Buy him a Rainier.

sources.title: Seattle tech layoffs add up as smaller job cuts mount

title: The Robes in the Window Are Not a Halloween Prop
dek: Downtown Reddit freaked out. The man who put them there wants you to stay uncomfortable.
body: Walk past the Dexter Horton Building at 2nd and Cherry and you might catch something that stops you cold: Ku Klux Klan robes, visible through a window in Suite 300. A Reddit user posted photos asking what the hell was going on, and some commenters figured it was a tasteless Halloween display.

It isn't. The robes belong to the American History Traveling Museum: The Unspoken Truths, curated by Delbert Richardson, which tells American history through an Afrocentric lens. Its sections run Mother Africa, American Chattel Slavery, The Jim Crow Era, and Still We Rise.
> Everything I do is intentional (Delbert Richardson)
Richardson told KUOW the discomfort is the point: if you're uncomfortable and you want to grow, stay there. And he says the adults are where the work is needed.

The Sinner's take: in a city that loves to call itself progressive, a little discomfort is overdue. Go see it. It's open 1 to 5 p.m. on select Wednesdays through December, including October 21 and 28.

sources.title: 'Everything I do is intentional.' Why Ku Klux Klan robes are displayed in downtown Seattle

title: KEXP Eyes the Haight
dek: Seattle's station is flirting with a second home in San Francisco. Breathe. It's not moving.
body: KEXP started in 1972 as KCMU, a student station at the University of Washington. Now it's looking at a landmark at Haight and Ashbury. A proposed partnership with SF Heritage and the Blue Bear School of Music would turn the 1903 Doolan-Larson House, San Francisco Landmark No. 253, into a music and culture center.

The early sketch includes broadcast studios, a rooftop venue, space for music lessons and a public hangout. KEXP already has a Bay Area foothold: it won 92.7 KREV FM, now KEXC, at a bankruptcy auction in late 2023 with a $3.75 million bid.
> Art and music have been part of what makes San Francisco special for generations. (San Francisco Mayor Daniel Lurie)
Nothing's final. Next comes community feedback, a reuse plan, and the boring part with financing.

Is it a little weird watching our station flirt with California? Sure. But the rooftop venue sounds great, and if a Seattle institution gets to plant a flag where the Summer of Love happened, that's a win for us too. Just don't forget who raised you, KEXP.

sources.title: Seattle's KEXP eyes a second physical home in San Francisco's historic Haight-Ashbury

title: Lights Out on 15th
dek: Three Capitol Hill favorites shut overnight. Blame the bricks, the leases and an unpaid tax bill.
body: One building, three closings. Bar Vacilando, Rione XIII and Rubinstein Bagels all lived at 401 15th Ave E. Rione XIII and Rubinstein shut immediately. Bar Vacilando got one last Saturday.

Ethan Stowell's One House Hospitality, which ran Rione XIII, said ongoing building problems made it impossible to keep going. An August code complaint described crumbling bricks along the facade on the East Harrison side. A later city inspection found the brick facade 'stable,' according to a Capitol Hill Seattle Blog headline.
Then there's the money. According to King County records cited in the coverage, the property hasn't paid taxes since 2023 and owes more than $135,000 through 2026.
Rione XIII ran 14 years. Bar Vacilando had just marked a decade on the block. That's a lot of Negronis and a lot of first dates, gone overnight because the walls and the books both crumbled.
Raise one tonight for 15th Ave E. And landlords, fix your bricks.

sources.outlet: Hoodline, summarizing Capitol Hill Seattle Blog
